KEY MESSAGE 1...Daily chances for showers and thunderstorms 
will return Monday and into the middle of the week. There is a 
risk for strong to severe thunderstorms during the week, as well
as a marginal risk for localized heavy rainfall leading to 
flash flooding.

A mid-level shortwave trough will approach the area Monday 
afternoon into the evening as mean flow shifts more westerly and
mid-level flow increases amid falling heights. The timing of 
this synoptic evolution has continued to be a bit earlier with 
the recent guidance for Monday. This mid-level shortwave trough 
will be moving in from the west which means it will initiate 
showers and thunderstorms off to our west Monday morning. 
Currently, model guidance decays this activity before it reaches
our area and keeps it off to the west. Monday's convection 
potential will at least partially depend on what occurs upstream
of our area through the day. 

For this update, SPC has maintained the Marginal (level 1 out 
of 5) Risk for severe thunderstorms for much of our forecast 
area for Monday. The Slight (level 2 out of 5) Risk was expanded
east today right to our forecast area border. There remains 
uncertainty around Monday, but an additional expansion further 
east into our forecast area is possible if trends continue to 
hold. Given the recent trends among CAM guidance and model 
soundings, the primary risk is damaging wind gusts as there 
looks to be more of an upscale growth potential into a line 
segment as the activity approaches our area. Instability and 
low-level lapse rates are supportive of severe weather along 
with increasing bulk shear values for storm organization. 
Another note, there could also be a non-zero tornado threat as 
well as model guidance shows low- level shear increasing during 
the afternoon and evening. However, there remains a bit of 
uncertainty around how some of thermodynamics evolve through 
Monday afternoon and evening. 

In terms of flash flooding, there is a Marginal (level 1 out 4)
Risk for excessive rainfall for areas mainly near and northwest
of the I- 95 corridor. PWATs do look to increase again to 
upwards of 2 inches, so there is the heavy rain potential. 
However, with a more linear storm mode being possible, this will
lead to a more progressive storm motion as the mid-level flow 
increases Monday. One takeaway with this forecast update is 
there remains uncertainty around the timing of the convection. 
Variations remain among model guidance and what happens for our 
forecast area will also depend on what happens upstream to our 
north and west with that convective development.

Recent forecast trends have resulted in lower instability 
compared to previous runs on Tuesday given the faster evolution 
of the synoptic features (cold front and shortwave trough). 
Essentially, it looks like Tuesday's activity will be shunted to
our southwest compared to previous forecasts based on the 
latest synoptic trends. With that said, we could still see some 
convection potential or even get the remnants of whatever occurs
upstream later in the evening. So while the threat of severe 
storms now appears to be lessening for Tuesday, we could still 
get showers and storms in some form. Details for Tuesday are 
even more uncertain than Monday, and Monday's activity will 
probably play some role in what exactly happens Tuesday.

A cold front looks to stall to our northwest Tuesday into 
Wednesday. Multiple waves look to ride along the stalled 
boundary which will support diurnally driven convection 
continuing at least through Thursday. The front looks to push 
through by late Thursday and a much drier and cooler airmass 
will arrive by Friday and Saturday as a result, which will bring
us a more pronounced break in convective potential and more 
pleasant weather conditions.


KEY MESSAGE 2...Hot and humid conditions will persist into the 
middle of the week, but humidity will not be as oppressive as 
recent days.

A relatively stagnant synoptic pattern will remain in place 
across our region. Quasi zonal mid and upper level flow will be 
in place through the middle of the week as Bermuda high pressure
persists offshore. This will keep a very warm and moist airmass
in place across the region through the period.

Hot and humid conditions will continue for the next several 
days. A weak cold front passing through the area today will 
continue to usher in slightly drier air and allow dewpoints to 
mix out some during the afternoon hours both today and Monday. 
This will give some slight reprieve from the excessive humidity 
we've experienced in recent days, though highs will still be in 
the upper 80s to low or even mid 90s. The lower dewpoints will 
result in maximum heat indices mainly in the mid to upper 90s, 
though could get near 100 degrees in Delmarva and near the coast
in New Jersey. Since the forecast is decidedly below criteria,
